No statements after the TopBuild closing; MATERIAL; The latest balance sheet is dated 30 June 2026, one day before TopBuild closed, and no third-quarter 2026 report is supplied; the latest quarter ended 128 days before the as-of date. Debt principal of USD 6,111 million at that date, including USD 11 million drawn on the ABL facility, already counts the USD 3.0 billion of escrowed notes, while the USD 3.0 billion incremental term loan of 1 July 2026, the USD 1.0 billion of Series C preferred equity issued at closing and the acquired business appear in no supplied balance sheet. Net debt, leverage and liquidity from these sources are pre-TopBuild measures; The quarterly report for the quarter ending 30 September 2026, or a filing that gives the post-closing balance sheet

TopBuild results and pro forma combination not supplied; MATERIAL; TopBuild's own statements and any pro forma combined results are absent, and the quarterly report states that initial accounting is incomplete with no provisional amounts for assets acquired or liabilities assumed. The pro forma tables cover Beacon and Kodiak only, so earnings and leverage of the enlarged company cannot be built from these sources; The report that carries the preliminary purchase price allocation, or a filing with TopBuild's historical and pro forma financial information

Executed debt documents not supplied; MINOR; Covenant, guarantor, collateral and restricted-payment terms rest on the summaries in the notes, including the 1.0 to 1.0 springing fixed charge coverage test on the ABL facility. Legal & covenants cannot be assessed from executed text and Fundamental credit must describe the terms as summarised; The indentures and supplemental indentures, the term loan and ABL credit agreements and the 1 July 2026 amendment

Beacon predecessor information not supplied; MINOR; Beacon is the predecessor for financial reporting, so results before 29 April 2025 are the company's own and exclude Beacon, and the exhibits that carry Beacon's results for 1 January to 28 April 2025 and for 2024 are not in the set. Full-year 2025 contains Beacon for about eight months, so year-on-year comparisons are not like for like. Pro forma net sales and net loss are given for 2025 and 2024, nine months 2025 and the second quarter and first half of 2025, but no pro forma EBITDA, margins or balance sheet; The predecessor exhibits to the annual report and the quarterly reports

Proxy statement not supplied; MINOR; Directors, independence, compensation, beneficial ownership and related-party items are incorporated by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied, so Business & governance is limited to what the annual report and quarterly reports state; The 2026 proxy statement

Mixed rounding basis; MINOR; The annual report and the first-quarter 2026 release print one decimal while the second-quarter 2026 report and release print whole millions. Derived sums differ from printed figures by up to USD 0.4 million of net sales, which is rounding but must be disclosed wherever a figure is derived; State the rounding basis beside each derived figure

Kodiak price differs between filings; MINOR; The annual report gives a headline price of about USD 2.25 billion with 13.2 million shares and the fourth-quarter release repeats the USD 2.25 billion, while the second-quarter report gives a net purchase price of USD 2.22 billion with 13.3 million shares including 0.1 million rollover shares. facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: The leverage picture turns on three choices the reader must make. Net debt of USD 3,266 million at 30 June 2026 is 9.45x reported EBITDA and 4.51x adjusted EBITDA, and USD 3,000 million of it is the escrowed notes counted as debt while the matching cash is restricted and outside the cash figure; with the escrow counted, net debt would be USD 266 million. Excluding the escrow, net debt rose from USD 12.3 million at 31 March 2026 to USD 266 million at 30 June 2026. The real step-up is the incremental term loan of USD 3,000 million drawn on 1 July 2026, which lifts standalone net debt to USD 6,266 million before any TopBuild earnings are counted, so creditors should treat the reported ratios as a floor on post-closing leverage, not a measure of it. facts.text: Data-quality and definition risks are limited but real. No balance sheet, TopBuild statements or purchase price allocation after 2026-07-01; High; Post-closing net debt, leverage and interest cost are not established; the pro forma net debt of 6266 is a standalone adjustment to the 2026-06-30 balance sheet and no pro forma leverage is stated because TopBuild's earnings are not supplied; Obtain the report for the quarter ending 2026-09-30, which the company says will carry the preliminary allocation

Reported EBITDA is derived, not printed; Medium; Every ratio on reported EBITDA rests on a derivation from net income, taxes, net interest, depreciation and amortization; the issuer prints only adjusted EBITDA; Show reported and adjusted ratios side by side and state the derivation

Cash interest paid carries no coupon on the new debt; Medium; Cover at 2026-06-30 overstates what the larger debt will produce, because the 2031 and 2034 notes pay a first coupon on 2027-01-15 and the incremental term loan was drawn on 2026-07-01; Recompute cover when a period with the new debt in full is reported

Statement lines printed as a dash or absent in a period; Low; Dashes and missing lines are written as Not supplied and never as zero: loss on debt extinguishment, other income, deferred tax assets, revolver borrowings, mezzanine equity, common stock par and several financing lines in periods where the statement prints none; no subtotal depends on them, because every subtotal adds without them; None needed for the figures used

Rank across collateral pools is not established; Medium; The debt stack shows lien classes; priority between the ABL facility, the term loan and the 2032 notes depends on intercreditor terms that are not supplied; Obtain the executed debt documents before inferring priority or recovery
Capital expenditure split; Low; Maintenance and growth capital expenditures are not disclosed, so only total capital expenditures are used; None needed for the figures used

Segment revenue is not a schedule; Low; The company reports one operating segment and plans new segments after Kodiak and TopBuild; only sales by line of business are available, and no segment sum is stated; Re-read segment data once the new structure is reported

Balance sheets at 2025-09-30 and 2025-06-30 are not carried here; Low; Net debt and liquidity are stated at 2025-12-31, 2026-03-31 and 2026-06-30 only; the third-quarter 2025 report holds the 2025-09-30 balance sheet; Add the 2025-09-30 balance sheet if a longer net debt history is wanted

Restricted cash at 2025-12-31 is not located; Low; The cash-flow balance of 2365.4 exceeds balance-sheet cash of 2361.6 by 3.8 of restricted cash whose balance-sheet line is not stated; net debt uses balance-sheet cash; None needed for the figures used

facts.text: Control is concentrated in one founder group, which supports continuity of the acquisition strategy and removes outside challenge to it. facts.text: The preferred stack is the largest claim ahead of common equity and behind all debt, and its cash-pay features draw on the same cash as debt service. Liquidation preferences total USD 4,575 million. The Convertible Preferred pays 9%, which is USD 90.0 million a year, and Jacobs Private Equity II, LLC holds 90.00% of it; Series C pays 4.75%, which is USD 142.5 million a year at the full USD 3,000 million; and the Mandatory Convertible Preferred pays 5.50%. Series C is carried as mezzanine equity because holders can require cash redemption after a fundamental change, and a change of control would separately trigger a 101% repurchase offer on the notes, although the definitions are not supplied. facts.text: Beacon was the first acquisition and turned a software company into a building products distributor. It closed on 29 April 2025 for a net purchase price of USD 10,644 million, made up of USD 7,736 million for the shares, USD 104 million for converted equity awards and USD 2,948 million to repay Beacon's own debt, less USD 144 million of cash acquired. New debt at closing was USD 2,250 million of 6.75% senior secured notes due 2032 and a USD 2,250 million term loan, with an asset-based facility of up to USD 2,000 million alongside; equity raised around the closing came from private placements and public offerings. Beacon was determined to be the predecessor for financial reporting, but the statements supplied show the company's own results before 29 April 2025, which exclude Beacon. tables.limitation: Sponsor / Governance Risk Level: Medium. The risk level is driven by concentrated founder control and an acquisition-led funding pattern, because large debt-funded deals and cash-pay preferred stock can raise leverage and fixed charges faster than earnings grow, which implies higher event and refinancing risk for creditors. Countervailing evidence is the equity and preferred funding of the first two deals, the absence of documented extraction and stated covenant compliance. Further analysis requires the proxy statement, the executed debt and preferred documents and the first report after the TopBuild closing. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Fixed charges at the new debt level exceed what the pre-TopBuild earnings can carry, so the credit rests on TopBuild's contribution. Coupons on the debt outstanding at 30 June 2026 run at about USD 401 million a year against cash interest paid of USD 221.0 million, and at about USD 570 million with the incremental term loan at the existing term loan rate, which is an assumption because its margin is not stated. Adding about USD 264 million of preferred dividends gives about USD 834 million, or 0.87x of twelve-month adjusted EBITDA; adjusted EBITDA of about USD 1,140 million would be needed for 2.00x cover of interest alone, about USD 416 million more than the pre-TopBuild base. The first operational break is gross profit: repeating the 5.05% volume decline and a 1.0 percentage point margin loss for twelve months would remove about USD 216 million of adjusted EBITDA, 29.79% of the pre-TopBuild base, with little cost relief because many expenses are fixed.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C-06; calculation C-07; calculation C-17

facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The financial transmission runs through fixed charges that do not flex: the first coupons on the 2031 and 2034 notes fall due on 15 January 2027, interest runs at about USD 570 million a year and preferred dividends at about USD 264 million, so a seasonal half year at those charges would use about USD 511 million of cash, covered 9.20x by total liquidity of USD 4,704 million. Leverage is the casualty rather than liquidity: lower earnings against the added debt would push leverage above where it would otherwise be, by an amount that cannot be quantified because TopBuild's earnings are not supplied, and the 2031 to 2034 maturities of USD 9,100 million would then be refinanced from a weaker position. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, QXO presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, defensive demand, low customer concentration and liquidity of USD 4,704 million, but credit quality is constrained by leverage that cannot be established after the TopBuild closing, add-backs of 52.30% of adjusted EBITDA, falling organic sales and run-rate fixed charges of about USD 834 million. Cash-flow durability appears weak because free cash flow was USD 141.2 million over twelve months before acquisitions and preferred dividends and is negative in the first half. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on TopBuild's earnings, on the seasonal pattern and on whether acquisitions are held to what equity can fund; no principal falls due before 2030. The primary downside path is a weak first quarter of 2027 on the enlarged charges. Further analysis would require TopBuild's earnings, debt and cash, the margin on the incremental term loan and the first combined results. Top risk: leverage and fixed charges after the TopBuild closing, which no supplied document measures. The supplied documents support a credit snapshot of QXO as of 30 June 2026, not of the company after the TopBuild acquisition closed on 1 July 2026, because no later financial statements are supplied. ## Findings
### Bottom line

Net debt was 9.45x reported LTM EBITDA and 4.51x issuer-adjusted EBITDA at 30 June 2026, so creditor leverage depends on accepting add-backs that are 52.30% of adjusted EBITDA, and both ratios exclude TopBuild.
Basis: calculation C26; calculation C29; calculation C32

Gross debt at carrying value was USD 6,040 million against unrestricted cash of USD 2,774 million, so net debt was USD 3,266 million; that counts USD 3,000 million of escrowed notes as debt while their cash sits outside the cash figure, and it excludes the USD 3,000 million incremental term loan drawn on 1 July 2026. Cash interest paid over the twelve months covered reported EBITDA 1.56x and adjusted EBITDA 3.28x.
Basis: calculation C16; calculation C27; calculation C30; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 44; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 49

The earnings base is uneven by quarter: adjusted EBITDA was USD 301.9 million in the third quarter of 2025 and USD 1.2 million in the first quarter of 2026, so a single quarter should not be annualised.
Basis: 10-Q_2025-09-30_qxo-20250930.htm.jsonl, page 50; EX-99.1_2026-05-12_qxoq1-26earningsrelease.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62

### Financial interpretation

The leverage picture turns on three choices the reader must make. Net debt of USD 3,266 million at 30 June 2026 is 9.45x reported EBITDA and 4.51x adjusted EBITDA, and USD 3,000 million of it is the escrowed notes counted as debt while the matching cash is restricted and outside the cash figure; with the escrow counted, net debt would be USD 266 million. Excluding the escrow, net debt rose from USD 12.3 million at 31 March 2026 to USD 266 million at 30 June 2026. The real step-up is the incremental term loan of USD 3,000 million drawn on 1 July 2026, which lifts standalone net debt to USD 6,266 million before any TopBuild earnings are counted, so creditors should treat the reported ratios as a floor on post-closing leverage, not a measure of it.

Basis: calculation C15; calculation C16; calculation C42; calculation C40; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 44; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 49; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 54; EX-99.1_2026-08-13_qxoq2-26earningsrelease.htm.jsonl, page 8

Coverage is thin on reported earnings and adequate on adjusted earnings. Cash interest paid over the twelve months was USD 221.0 million, which covers reported EBITDA of USD 345.7 million 1.56x and adjusted EBITDA of USD 724.8 million 3.28x. Cash interest is also a floor on what the debt will cost: the notes issued in June 2026 pay a first coupon in January 2027 and the incremental term loan was drawn on 1 July 2026, so neither is in the interest paid to date, while the earnings base excludes TopBuild. Cover on the enlarged company cannot be judged until the combined earnings are reported.

spans.text: # CP-1A Business & governance: QXO, Inc. (qxo)
## Request

QXO, Inc. (issuer id qxo), as of 2026-11-05, credit snapshot pathway. Scope: business and operating model, transactions and new debt issues, ownership and control, governance, sponsor and shareholder behaviour, capital allocation and issuer history from the supplied filings and releases, with the latest period ending 30 June 2026 and events to 1 July 2026. No credit recommendation, peer ranking or recovery view is given.
## Sources
| Source | Document | Document date | sha256 | Use |

| 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended 31 December 2025 | 2026-02-27 | 1b7dee5c3907814ca02da7e5177715b488778f3cfe6a6a69dbb9a2d892ae7bd4 | Business, strategy, executive officers, voting concentration and board designation rights, dividends, financing history, audit report and internal-control assessment |

| 10-Q_2026-03-31_qxo-20260331.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 | 2026-05-12 | f661446a2ae3c415c83c14493e42b107a6ed744b45a540466d49f9056424d438 | TopBuild merger terms at signing, termination fee and the Kodiak closing |

| 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 June 2026 | 2026-08-14 | 894ff623087578f719301215adbe097ad733e1b300a9d2d5bf4a10f19be9a21b | Acquisition notes, preferred equity and warrant terms, debt note, restricted-payment disclosure, sales by line, cash flow statement and subsequent events |

| EX-99.1_2026-08-13_qxoq2-26earningsrelease.htm.jsonl | Earnings release (Exhibit 99.1) for the second quarter 2026 | 2026-08-13 | 67328156dff6e164d45723d576bcfc4e259ba15144552671032a5a2232707d03 | Sales by line of business, the restricted cash note and management statements on the EBITDA plan and market position |
| Supplied analysis | Module | sha256 | Use |
| Source readiness | CP-0 | ffb85fc512c998a8062881f8607b46e4b0f12066828db0fa8c2838076411b280 | Source gate, the perimeter break at 2026-07-01 and the missing-source gaps; no figure is taken from it |
## Findings
### Bottom line

QXO is a founder-controlled consolidator whose creditors are exposed to acquisition appetite rather than to extraction: preferred equity funded Kodiak, but new debt funded 40% of the roughly USD 15,000 million TopBuild purchase. Control sits with the founder, who held about 22.1% of the voting power, and his investment vehicle, which may designate 40% of the board. Preferred stock of USD 4,575 million at liquidation preference ranks ahead of common equity, and the three deals since April 2025 total about USD 27,866 million of price.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; calculation C-08; calculation C-11; calculation C-13

Apart from contractual preferred dividends, the filings show no related-party fees, distributions to the founder group or creditor-adverse refinancing, but the proxy statement that would disclose them is not supplied, and ownership percentages are stated only as of the annual report, before the 2026 share and preferred issuances.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 51; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

Control is concentrated in one founder group, which supports continuity of the acquisition strategy and removes outside challenge to it. Brad Jacobs held about 22.1% of the voting power at the date of the annual report, and Jacobs Private Equity II, LLC may designate 40% of the board for as long as the investors in the 2024 equity deal keep at least 30% of fully diluted votes, a share the company put at 39.4% at that date. The board includes a lead independent director, but the independence of the other directors is not stated, and no later filing updates these figures after the 2026 share and Series C issuances, so the headroom above the 30% threshold is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 34–35; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 111; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 87; calculation C-17

Acquisition funding follows no fixed policy, so leverage tolerance has to be read deal by deal. Beacon used USD 4,500 million of new debt against a net price of USD 10,644 million, a share of 42.28%, and USD 1,400 million of that debt was repaid within a month from equity proceeds; Kodiak used no new debt; TopBuild used USD 6,000 million against a price of about USD 15,000 million, a share of 40.00%. None of the seven documents states a leverage target, a credit-rating objective or a deleveraging plan after TopBuild; management states a plan to more than double EBITDA by 2030, which is a growth goal without a base year.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 52–55; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 46–49; EX-99.1_2026-08-13_qxoq2-26earningsrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C-02; calculation C-03; calculation C-05; calculation C-08

The preferred stack is the largest claim ahead of common equity and behind all debt, and its cash-pay features draw on the same cash as debt service. Liquidation preferences total USD 4,575 million. The Convertible Preferred pays 9%, which is USD 90.0 million a year, and Jacobs Private Equity II, LLC holds 90.00% of it; Series C pays 4.75%, which is USD 142.5 million a year at the full USD 3,000 million; and the Mandatory Convertible Preferred pays 5.50%. The company paid USD 84 million of preferred dividends in the first half of 2026, a half in which operating cash flow was negative. Series C is carried as mezzanine equity because holders can require cash redemption after a fundamental change, and a change of control would separately trigger a 101% repurchase offer on the notes, although the definitions are not supplied.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 36–38; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, pages 46–47; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62; calculation C-12; calculation C-13; calculation C-14; calculation C-15; calculation C-17; calculation C-20

No extraction, related-party payment or creditor-adverse liability management is documented beyond the contractual preferred dividends, and that finding is limited to what the filings disclose. The only common dividend was USD 17.4 million in June 2024, before any acquisition, and the company says it does not intend to pay another; the only change to existing debt terms described, apart from the new incremental loan, is a cut in the term loan margin from 3.00% to 2.00%. The company calls the limits on restricted payments not significant given that policy, so creditors should not treat those limits as a binding check on distributions.

The business is defensive in demand and seasonal in cash flow. The company states that about 80% of industry revenue is repair and re-roofing, no customer exceeded 1% of 2025 net sales, and the first quarter is expected to bring low profit or a loss. Complementary products reached 37.9% of second-quarter 2026 net sales, with Kodiak contributing USD 595 million of the total, against 22.4% in the second quarter of 2025, which held Beacon for only two months; supplier concentration is not quantified.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 10–12; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 55; calculation C-18; calculation C-19

Reporting quality is adequate for a listed filer but leaves gaps that matter to a creditor. The auditor's opinion on 2025 is unmodified with one critical audit matter on the valuation of Beacon's customer relationships; management excluded Beacon, which was 86.1% of consolidated assets and 99.1% of revenue, from its internal-control assessment as the rules allow for one year, so no auditor attestation on internal control exists; and the purchase price allocation for TopBuild is not yet available.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a cautious view is how the first two deals were funded. Debt remaining after the May 2025 prepayment covered 29.12% of the Beacon price, with the rest met from equity and cash; USD 1,450 million raised in May 2025 exceeded the USD 1,400 million prepayment; and Kodiak needed no new debt because Series C preferred stock covered its cash cost with USD 28 million to spare. The only cash flowing to the founder group in the filings is its contractual share of preferred dividends, USD 81.0 million a year, and the preferred investors hold instruments that rank behind every creditor.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 48; calculation C-03; calculation C-04; calculation C-06; calculation C-17

Three developments would raise the risk assessment: a further acquisition funded mainly with debt, evidence that cash is moved from the borrowing group to the parent to pay preferred dividends outside the restricted-payment limits, or related-party arrangements and board-seat rights for the Series C investors that the supplied documents do not show. Three would lower it: a stated leverage target together with repayment of the incremental term loan, conversion of preferred stock into common shares, which would end the cash dividends but dilute control, and a proxy statement that discloses an independent board majority and no related-party payments.
### Limitations

- The control conclusion rests on voting and designation percentages stated at the annual report date; if the 2026 issuances have taken the investors' fully diluted share below the 30% threshold, the founder group's board designation right would shrink and the concentration finding would weaken.

- The no-extraction finding covers only what the filings and notes disclose; the independence of most directors, related-party transactions, compensation and fees sit in a proxy statement that is not supplied, so a related-party payment would not be visible and the finding could reverse.

- The finding that creditor protections are limited relies on the company's summaries of the debt and preferred documents; if the executed documents define permitted holders or restricted-payment baskets more tightly than summarised, the view that distributions are unchecked would soften.

- TopBuild is described only by its purchase terms, so the operating model and the funding conclusion cover the business before 1 July 2026; the stated price also differs between filings, which makes the 40% debt share an approximation.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

Beacon was the first acquisition and turned a software company into a building products distributor. It closed on 29 April 2025 for a net purchase price of USD 10,644 million, made up of USD 7,736 million for the shares, USD 104 million for converted equity awards and USD 2,948 million to repay Beacon's own debt, less USD 144 million of cash acquired. New debt at closing was USD 2,250 million of 6.75% senior secured notes due 2032 and a USD 2,250 million term loan, with an asset-based facility of up to USD 2,000 million alongside; equity raised around the closing came from private placements and public offerings. Beacon was determined to be the predecessor for financial reporting, but the statements supplied show the company's own results before 29 April 2025, which exclude Beacon.

Two capital moves in 2025 reduced the debt taken for Beacon and its cost. A voluntary prepayment of USD 1,400 million on 29 May 2025, funded from the May equity and preferred offerings, left USD 850 million of term loan, and a repricing on 5 November 2025 cut the Term SOFR margin from 3.00% to 2.00%. On 27 May 2025 the company also issued 5.50% Series B Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock for USD 558 million net, a USD 575 million claim that must convert into common shares.

Countervailing evidence is the equity and preferred funding of the first two deals, the absence of documented extraction and stated covenant compliance. ## Findings
### Bottom line

QXO's fundamental credit is adequate before the TopBuild closing and cannot be fully assessed after it: liquidity and maturities are comfortable, but the leverage that matters rests on an acquired earnings base that no supplied document reports.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C-01; calculation C-15; calculation C-18

Net leverage at 30 June 2026 was 4.51x issuer-adjusted EBITDA and 9.45x reported EBITDA, and pro forma net leverage after the incremental term loan is not established. Run-rate interest of about USD 570 million, assuming the new loan costs what the existing term loan does, and preferred dividends of about USD 264 million together exceed twelve-month adjusted EBITDA of USD 724.8 million, so TopBuild's earnings must carry the structure while organic sales are falling.

### Key findings

Leverage after the TopBuild closing is not established, and the pre-closing ratios are a floor rather than a measure. Net debt was USD 3,266 million at 30 June 2026, USD 6,266 million after the USD 3,000 million incremental term loan drawn on 1 July 2026, and USD 3,289 million after the USD 23 million Convertible Preferred dividend paid after the quarter end; net leverage was 4.51x adjusted and 9.45x reported EBITDA, and pro forma net leverage is not established. The ratios exclude TopBuild's earnings, cash and debt and count USD 3,000 million of escrowed notes as debt without their cash, so they cannot show where leverage lands once combined results are reported.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 44; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 49; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 54; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C-01

Fixed charges at the new debt level exceed what the pre-TopBuild earnings can carry, so the credit rests on TopBuild's contribution. Coupons on the debt outstanding at 30 June 2026 run at about USD 401 million a year against cash interest paid of USD 221.0 million, and at about USD 570 million with the incremental term loan at the existing term loan rate, which is an assumption because its margin is not stated. Adding about USD 264 million of preferred dividends gives about USD 834 million, or 0.87x of twelve-month adjusted EBITDA; adjusted EBITDA of about USD 1,140 million would be needed for 2.00x cover of interest alone, about USD 416 million more than the pre-TopBuild base. About 42.38% of principal is floating after the incremental loan, and a rise of 100 bp adds about USD 39 million of interest a year; Series C dividends of USD 142.5 million can be paid in shares, which is the main cash lever.

Earnings quality is the second constraint, because more than half of adjusted EBITDA is add-backs. Add-backs were USD 379.1 million of USD 724.8 million of twelve-month adjusted EBITDA, 52.30%, and USD 514.1 million against reported EBITDA of USD 133.7 million in FY2025; transaction costs of USD 52 million and transformation costs of USD 24 million were added back in the second quarter of 2026 alone. The company defines the adjustments itself, so reported EBITDA of USD 345.7 million is the conservative base; stock-based compensation is the one recurring item, and the other five add-backs, 71.90% of the FY2025 total, follow the acquisitions and should shrink as integration ends.

The trading trend is weaker than the reported sales growth suggests. Excluding Kodiak, net sales were 1.56% below the company's pro forma prior year in the second quarter of 2026 and 5.05% below in the first half; adjusted gross margin fell by 0.6 percentage points in the quarter and 1.0 percentage points in the half, because product cost rose faster than selling prices; and the adjusted EBITDA margin was 8.38% against 10.70% a year earlier. The chief executive says the second-quarter result reflects current market conditions; volume and price effects are not separated.

Replaying a seasonal half year at run-rate interest and preferred dividends would use about USD 511 million, covered 9.20x by that liquidity, so near-term distress is unlikely even before TopBuild's cash flow is counted, and the company states that liquidity is sufficient for the next 12 months.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a cautious view is that the structure is funded and not close to any test. Liquidity covers a replayed seasonal outflow 9.20x, no principal is due before 2030, the ABL covenant is not in force, the first two deals were paid largely with equity, preferred stock and cash, and tangible assets of USD 12,052 million cover gross debt 2.00x; TopBuild also adds an earnings base that is in no ratio, so if its earnings are large against the USD 3,000 million of added debt, leverage could fall below the pre-closing 4.51x on adjusted EBITDA. Most of the add-backs are tied to the acquisitions and should fall as integration ends.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C-02; calculation C-14; calculation C-16; calculation C-20

Three developments would raise the risk assessment: a first combined report showing net leverage above the pre-closing level on adjusted EBITDA, organic sales still falling with adjusted gross margin below its second-quarter level, or ABL drawings to fund the first-quarter seasonal outflow. Three would lower it: combined results showing net leverage below the pre-closing level, a return to organic growth with stable gross margin, and cash dividends cut through share payment or early repayment of the incremental term loan.
### Limitations

- No TopBuild earnings, cash or debt are supplied, so leverage and cover after the closing are bounds rather than measurements; if TopBuild's contribution is large against the added debt, the conclusion that fixed charges exceed the earnings base would reverse.

- The margin on the incremental term loan is not stated, so the interest estimate assumes the existing term loan rate; a higher margin would deepen the shortfall in cover and a lower one would narrow it.

- The organic sales trend rests on the company's unaudited pro forma net sales for Beacon, which do not separate volume from price; if that base is overstated, the decline would be smaller and the trading conclusion weaker.

- No ratings, dated market quotes or peer set are supplied and the only market input is the fair value of the debt at 30 June 2026, so the comparison with other leveraged distributors is qualitative and the view of refinancing capacity rests on maturities, liquidity and that single pricing point.

- The downside figures repeat observed first-half 2026 trends on the pre-TopBuild base and pair them with post-closing charges; if the enlarged business behaves differently, the scenario outcome moves in either direction.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Liquidity and maturities give the structure time. Total liquidity of USD 4,704 million at 30 June 2026 covers a replayed seasonal half year at run-rate charges 9.20x, no principal falls due before 2030, and the springing ABL test is not in force, so a weak season would be absorbed before any covenant or refinancing pressure arises.

### Company description

QXO is a distributor of roofing, waterproofing and complementary building products in North America that grew from a small software business through three acquisitions in 14 months. In the second quarter of 2026 residential roofing was 39.0% of net sales, non-residential roofing 22.7% and complementary products 37.9%, and TopBuild adds insulation distribution and installation from 1 July 2026, so the mix is moving away from roofing and dilutes the demand evidence the business has built up.

Demand is mostly repair and re-roofing, which the company puts at about 80% of industry revenue with new construction the remaining 20%; that supports cash-flow visibility and debt service in a downturn, but results are seasonal and the earnings history is not clean, because Beacon is in the figures from 29 April 2025, Kodiak from 1 April 2026 and TopBuild not at all. Customers are many and small, so credit exposure to any one account is low, and about 97% of net sales are in the United States.

### Ownership and group structure

Control is concentrated: the founder held about 22.1% of voting power and his investment vehicle may designate 40% of the board while the 2024 investors keep at least 30% of fully diluted votes, figures stated as of the annual report and not updated for the 2026 issuances. The debt sits at the operating subsidiary, QXO Building Products, with Holdings pledging the borrower's equity and subsidiary guarantors behind each facility, while preferred and common equity are issued by QXO, Inc.; the filings do not say how cash reaches the parent to pay preferred dividends or whether the parent guarantees the debt. For creditors the points to monitor are the route of cash from the borrowing group to the parent and the restricted-payment limits, which the company calls not significant.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Volume follows repair and re-roofing demand, housing starts and weather, so revenue is need-driven but not contractually recurring: the filings describe a transactional distribution model with volume rebates and give no contract duration or renewal data. Organic net sales were 1.56% below the pro forma prior year in the second quarter of 2026 and 5.05% below in the first half, so recent evidence is of falling volume or price rather than of durability, and the company attributes the result to current market conditions without separating volume from price.

Pricing power is partial. The company states that it has generally passed on manufacturers' price increases but that timing depends on competitive conditions, and gross margin fell in the second quarter as product cost rose faster than selling prices; customer concentration is low and supplier concentration high, so price discipline depends on the competitive pricing environment more than on switching costs, which the filings do not quantify.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Selling, general and administrative expense was 20.0% of net sales in the second quarter of 2026 against 24.0% a year earlier, helped by lower stock-based compensation, restructuring and transaction costs than in the prior-year quarter, while the company states that many expenses are fixed. The first operational consequence is operating leverage in both directions: a fall in volume cuts gross profit with little cost relief, so repeating the first-half 2026 trends for twelve months would remove about USD 216 million of adjusted EBITDA, 29.79% of the pre-TopBuild base. Margin defence relies on price pass-through and on integration savings that the company does not quantify, and restructuring costs of USD 24 million and transformation costs of USD 36 million added back in the first half show that savings are still being paid for.

### Capital intensity and free cash flow conversion

Capital expenditure was 1.14% of FY2025 net sales, so the model is asset-light and cash conversion is set by working capital, interest and acquisition costs rather than by capex. Free cash flow was USD 141.2 million over twelve months, 19.48% of adjusted EBITDA, before acquisitions and preferred dividends, and operating cash flow was negative in the first half of 2026 because receivables and inventories built ahead of the peak season; cash paid for income taxes was small at USD 5 million in the first half. Lease liabilities of USD 997 million sit outside the debt figures and about 97% of branches are leased, so occupancy cost is a fixed claim that competes with debt service in a downturn; EBITDA converts to free cash flow poorly today, and conversion falls further once run-rate interest and preferred dividends are counted.

### Competitive forces

Rivalry is meaningful but the industry is fragmented: the company describes thousands of small distributors alongside specialty distributors and big-box retailers competing on availability, technical advice, delivery, price and credit, and claims scale as the largest publicly traded roofing distributor. Scale helps purchasing and rebates, but the filings give no market-share, retention or entry-barrier data, so the strength of the moat is not established, and substitutes are not evidenced as a threat.

Buyer power is limited by customer fragmentation, since no customer exceeded 1% of net sales, although contractors can move volume on price. Supplier power is meaningful: three suppliers each supplied at least 10% of purchases and nearly 35% together, suppliers allocate product in shortages, and vendor rebates that lower cost can be changed; the effect lands on gross margin and fill rates rather than on solvency, but it is the force most likely to reach earnings quickly.

### Macro and policy factors

Economic and policy factors are material, and social and technological factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver based on the provided materials. Housing starts, business investment, interest rates and credit availability drive the new-construction and non-residential lines, and severe weather moves re-roofing demand in either direction; tariffs on steel and imported goods raise supplier prices and, if not passed on in time, margin. Higher interest rates also raise cost on floating debt: 42.38% of principal is floating after the incremental term loan and the supplied documents disclose no hedges.
### Credit SWOT

Strengths in credit terms are scale across a broad contractor base, liquidity with no principal due before 2030, equity and preferred funding beneath the debt, and a capital-light model. Weaknesses are leverage that is not established after the closing, fixed charges of about USD 834 million at run rate, add-backs of 52.30% of adjusted EBITDA, falling organic sales and a seasonal cash trough.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C-02; calculation C-06; calculation C-12; calculation C-15; calculation C-18

Opportunities that could improve credit quality are TopBuild earnings and integration savings that lower leverage, dividends on Series C stock paid in shares, and conversion of preferred stock that would end cash dividends. Threats that could weaken it are a soft housing or re-roofing season, tariff and asphalt cost shocks that are not passed on, a further debt-funded acquisition, failed integration of three businesses and higher rates on floating debt.

### Financial profile and credit quality

On the nine dimensions the evidence supports the following assessments. Scale and market position are strong, with USD 9,898.2 million of twelve-month net sales and the largest publicly traded roofing distribution business in North America on the company's description. Competitive advantage is average, because scale supports purchasing but no market-share, retention or switching-cost data are supplied. Business diversification is average: customers are diversified and the mix is broadening, but nearly 35% of purchases come from three suppliers and about 97% of sales are in one country. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since capex is light but many expenses are fixed. Margin stability is weak, with adjusted gross margin down and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 8.38% against 10.70%. Free cash flow stability is weak, at 19.48% of adjusted EBITDA before preferred dividends. Ability to refinance is average, helped by no principal due before 2030 and by fair values of the notes above par at 30 June 2026, and held back by leverage that is not established. Liquidity position is strong at 30 June 2026, at USD 4,704 million, and not established after the closing. Financial policy and governance is average: equity funded the first two deals, but no leverage target is stated and control is concentrated.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over 12 to 24 months the outlook turns on the first combined results for the quarter ending 30 September 2026, the first coupons on the 2031 and 2034 notes on 15 January 2027, which add to interest paid, and the first seasonal low with the enlarged charges. The company must show organic stabilisation and integration savings while restructuring and transformation costs are still being incurred, and the preferred stack adds about USD 264 million a year of dividends once Series C is fully issued.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 46; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C-12; calculation C-28

Over three to five years the management goal is to more than double EBITDA by 2030 and reach USD 50 billion of revenue within the decade, which is management language without a base year. The Series B preferred dividends end in May 2028, and USD 9,100 million of principal falls due between 2031 and 2034, USD 3,100 million of it on 30 April 2032, so refinancing is back-ended but concentrated. Sector tailwinds the company cites are a large housing shortage and an ageing housing stock that sustains repair demand; headwinds are the cyclicality of new construction, weather, tariffs and interest rates, and the company-specific headwinds are the integration of three businesses and the cost of the preferred stack.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 44; EX-99.1_2026-08-13_qxoq2-26earningsrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C-18; calculation C-26; calculation C-29
### Downside scenario

The downside that fits this issuer is a repeat of first-half 2026 trading on the enlarged capital structure. The initiating condition is a soft housing and re-roofing season in the first quarter of 2027, the seasonal low, with organic volume falling again and selling prices lagging cost increases from asphalt, steel or tariffs. The first operational break is gross profit: repeating the 5.05% volume decline and a 1.0 percentage point margin loss for twelve months would remove about USD 216 million of adjusted EBITDA, 29.79% of the pre-TopBuild base, with little cost relief because many expenses are fixed.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_qxo-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; calculation C-06; calculation C-07; calculation C-17

The financial transmission runs through fixed charges that do not flex: the first coupons on the 2031 and 2034 notes fall due on 15 January 2027, interest runs at about USD 570 million a year and preferred dividends at about USD 264 million, so a seasonal half year at those charges would use about USD 511 million of cash, covered 9.20x by total liquidity of USD 4,704 million. Leverage is the casualty rather than liquidity: lower earnings against the added debt would push leverage above where it would otherwise be, by an amount that cannot be quantified because TopBuild's earnings are not supplied, and the 2031 to 2034 maturities of USD 9,100 million would then be refinanced from a weaker position.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C-09; calculation C-12; calculation C-15; calculation C-16; calculation C-18

Management levers are real but limited: Series C dividends of USD 142.5 million can be paid in shares, there is no common dividend, capital expenditure is only 1.14% of net sales and so offers little, and ABL availability of USD 1,930 million and a history of raising equity are the main backstops. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress within the next 12 months, as the company also states, but not sufficient to show deleveraging. Primary downside path: a weak first quarter of 2027 on top of the first full burden of new interest and preferred dividends, before TopBuild's earnings are shown to carry them.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-06-30_qxo-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 62; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C-05; calculation C-12; calculation C-14
### Overall credit view

Overall, QXO presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, defensive demand, low customer concentration and liquidity of USD 4,704 million, but credit quality is constrained by leverage that cannot be established after the TopBuild closing, add-backs of 52.30% of adjusted EBITDA, falling organic sales and run-rate fixed charges of about USD 834 million. Cash-flow durability appears weak because free cash flow was USD 141.2 million over twelve months before acquisitions and preferred dividends and is negative in the first half. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on TopBuild's earnings, on the seasonal pattern and on whether acquisitions are held to what equity can fund; no principal falls due before 2030. The primary downside path is a weak first quarter of 2027 on the enlarged charges. Further analysis would require TopBuild's earnings, debt and cash, the margin on the incremental term loan and the first combined results. Top risk: leverage and fixed charges after the TopBuild closing, which no supplied document measures.
